sections.overview: Anopheles gambiae sensu stricto is a mosquito native to sub-Saharan Africa, including Madagascar. It is one of the region’s most efficient malaria vectors, although Plasmodium parasites cause the disease.
sections.identification: The adult is a small, slender mosquito, usually light brown to grey with pale and dark scales on the wings. Species accounts give adult wing lengths of about 2.8–4.4 mm; this is a wing measurement, not body length. Males have bushy, feathery antennae, whereas females’ antennae are less plume-like. A laboratory study found mean wing lengths of 2.84–2.91 mm in females and 2.73–2.92 mm in males across two years. These overlapping sample means do not establish a reliable sex difference in overall size; body height, width, and mass were not reported.
sections.habitat: The immature stages develop in shallow standing water, especially sunlit pools, puddles, hoof prints, marshes, and water-filled structures; larvae lie parallel to the surface to breathe.
sections.diet: Both adult sexes take nectar and other plant sugars, but only females blood-feed on vertebrates to obtain protein for egg production. Anopheles gambiae sensu stricto strongly favours human hosts. Its larvae filter algae and organic particles from water.
sections.behavior: Adults are active at night, with high biting activity often recorded after midnight and before dawn. Females may enter houses to feed and rest, though outdoor feeding and resting also occur.
sections.reproduction: Females lay eggs one by one directly on water; each egg has lateral floats and does not tolerate drying. A laying may contain 50–300 eggs, and eggs usually hatch within two or three days. Development from egg to adult can take about 10–11 days in warm conditions, but up to three weeks when cooler.
sections.ecology: The name Anopheles gambiae is also used loosely for a complex containing several closely related sibling species. Anopheles coluzzii and Anopheles arabiensis look almost identical externally but can differ in host choice, resting behaviour, and vector importance.
sections.conservation: Its ecological importance is its role in transmitting human malaria, though Plasmodium parasites rather than the mosquito cause the disease. An infected female can pass the parasites during a later blood meal.
